A2.01.goal: Introduce yourself as a physics student, ask basic questions and understand a course timetable.
notes: The verb be
Use I am, you/we/they are, and he/she/it is. Make a question by moving be before the subject: “Is this the laboratory?”
Present-simple routines
Use the base verb after I/you/we/they, but add -s for he/she/it: “She studies physics.”
Questions
Use do or does with ordinary present-simple verbs: “Does she study physics?” The main verb stays in the base form.
Academic etiquette
Use a clear subject line, a greeting, a concise question and a polite closing in an email to an instructor.
A2.01.pronunciation: Practise spelling names and email addresses aloud. Say @ as “at” and . as “dot.”

A2.02.goal: Read, write, compare and pronounce scientific quantities and SI units.
notes: Scientific quantities
A quantity is what is measured (for example, mass); a unit expresses its value (for example, kilogram, symbol kg).
Numbers in spoken English
Read 0.05 as “zero point zero five.” Distinguish thirteen from thirty and read 1/2 as “one-half” or “a half.”
Countable and uncountable
Say “three measurements” but “some equipment.” Use how many with countable plurals and how much with uncountable nouns.
SI conventions
Write a space between numbers and SI unit symbols: 2 m, 4.5 V. Unit symbols are not pluralized and capitalization matters (K is kelvin; k is a prefix).
A2.02.pronunciation: Practise thirteen/thirty, decimal points, fractions, and grouped quantity-plus-unit phrases.

A2.03.goal: Identify apparatus and describe where items are located in a labelled teaching room.
notes: There is / there are
Use there is for one item and there are for more than one. Ask “Is there a ruler?” and “Are there two timers?”
Position words
Use on, under, between, next to, behind, in front of, on the left and on the right. State the viewing direction before giving relative positions.
Near and far
This/these refer to nearby objects; that/those refer to more distant objects. Match singular and plural.
Instructions
Sequence actions with first, next, then and finally. This lesson uses paper cards or disconnected apparatus only.
A2.03.pronunciation: Pay attention to this/these and that/those; pronounce final plural -s clearly.

A2.04.goal: Describe routine physics activities and motion happening now.
notes: Present simple
Use it for habits, schedules and general statements: “The class meets every Tuesday.”
Present continuous
Use am/is/are + verb-ing to describe an action in progress: “The cart is moving right now.”
Motion verbs
Use rotate, rise, fall, speed up, slow down, stop and remain at rest when supported by the given source.
Evidence
Describe a displayed motion caption or data. Do not invent a velocity from an unlabeled still image.
A2.04.pronunciation: Practise linked phrases such as “is moving” and contrast stress on “usually” versus “now.”

A2.05.goal: Compare physical quantities and report differences without overclaiming.
notes: Comparatives
Compare two values with longer than, shorter than, higher than or more than. Do not use a superlative for a comparison between only two values.
Superlatives
For three or more values, use the highest, shortest or most useful when the comparison is justified.
Equality and sufficiency
Use as ... as, not as ... as, too short and long enough. Example: “The cable is long enough for this setup.”
Accuracy caution
Two close readings are not automatically accurate. Accuracy requires a reference or justified criterion.
A2.05.pronunciation: Read comparative endings clearly; say quantities with units before making comparisons.

A2.06.goal: Understand laboratory instructions, permissions and safety language.
notes: Obligation
Must and have to express requirements in the stated situation: “You must follow the instructor's instructions.”
Advice
Should expresses recommendations, not the same level of obligation as must.
Prohibition
Must not means an action is prohibited. Don't have to means it is not required; the two are not interchangeable.
Permission and requests
Use “Can I...?” or “Could you...?” for requests. Real laboratory rules always take precedence over fictional language exercises.
A2.06.pronunciation: Emphasize the word not in prohibitions. Practise polite rising intonation in requests.

A2.07.goal: Describe completed experiments and observations using the simple past.
notes: Simple past
Use the past form for completed events: “Yesterday we recorded the values.”
Regular verbs
Most regular past forms end in -ed, but pronunciation varies: /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/.
Irregular verbs
Learn high-frequency forms such as take/took, see/saw, write/wrote and make/made.
Reporting evidence
Write what was actually done or displayed, then separate observations from interpretations.
A2.07.pronunciation: Practise measured, checked and recorded; listen for the three pronunciations of -ed.

A2.08.goal: Explain what was happening when a classroom or virtual-lab event occurred.
notes: Past continuous
Use was/were + verb-ing for an ongoing activity in the past: “She was reading the display.”
Interrupted actions
Combine past continuous with simple past: “She was writing when the screen went dark.”
When and while
When often introduces the short event; while often introduces the ongoing background action.
Troubleshooting communication
State what happened, when it happened, and what you observed. Ask for clarification without guessing a cause.
A2.08.pronunciation: Group information into short phrases; practise contrastive stress in “was writing” versus “went dark.”

A2.09.goal: Discuss completed work, recent experience and unfinished assignments.
notes: Present perfect
Use have/has + past participle: “We have finished the table.”
Already, just and yet
Already describes completion, just often indicates very recent completion, and yet commonly appears in questions or negatives.
Experience
Use ever and never to ask about or describe experience, without inventing any laboratory result.
Time distinction
Use simple past with a specific finished time: “We finished on Monday.”
A2.09.pronunciation: Practise natural contractions (I've, she's, haven't) while keeping the full forms recognizable.

A2.10.goal: Explain simple physical causes and results, then state conditions and predictions.
notes: Because and so
Because introduces a reason; so introduces a result. Do not combine both carelessly for the same relationship.
Zero conditional
Use if + present simple, present simple for general rules under stated assumptions.
First conditional
Use if + present simple, will + base verb for a possible future result.
Physics assumptions
A model prediction is not a measured value. State conditions such as constant resistance or constant speed explicitly.
A2.10.pronunciation: Use a clear pause between conditional clauses; stress the physical assumption.

A2.11.goal: Describe simple graphs and distinguish observed trends from predictions.
notes: Axes and units
Always identify a horizontal and vertical quantity with units, such as Time (s) and Position (m).
Trends
Use increases, decreases, remains constant, rises and falls only for the shown interval.
Future statements
Use will or be going to for suitable predictions; neither one makes an unobserved value a measurement.
Difference and uncertainty
“Increased from 2 to 5” describes endpoints; “increased by 3” describes the difference. Use may, might and probably cautiously.
A2.11.pronunciation: Read graph axes aloud and clearly distinguish by from to when describing numerical changes.

A2.12.goal: Integrate A2 reading, grammar, mathematics and scientific explanation in a virtual experimental context.
notes: Before analysing
Read the apparatus description, quantities, units, observations and assumptions.
Describe the process
Use first, then, next and finally to describe a simple procedure.
Report results
Give measured or simulated values with their units, and distinguish an observation from a prediction.
Communicate the outcome
Explain your result simply, write a short paragraph and record a spoken summary for self-review once recording tools are available. This draft practice is not yet a final proficiency examination.
A2.12.pronunciation: Practise reading a quantity, its unit, and a full sentence explaining its meaning.
